Section 1

Brief and how it was met

Even after moving to the cloud, ABC Retail's order processing still leaned on custom pipelines and third-party messaging that delivered inconsistently and could not be scaled. This task replaces that with Azure Queue Storage for the work itself and an Azure file share for the operational record of what happened.

RequirementHow it is satisfied
Details relating to processing of orders stored in Azure Queues Placing an order puts a message on the order-processing queue, for example Processing order ORD-20260821-B11D for Michael Chen, 2 x Canvas Weekender Bag. The order is not complete until that message is handled.
Details relating to inventory management stored in Azure Queues Catalogue and stock movements go to inventory-management, including Uploading image "7d727e6c...jpg", Inventory item created, Stock adjusted and Inventory item removed.
Log files stored using Azure Files Every action is appended to logs/app-YYYY-MM-DD.log on the application-logs share. Generated inventory reports are written to exports/ on the same share.

Section 2

How work moves through the system

The queue is not a record of what already happened. It is what causes the work to happen, which is the distinction that makes the design worth anything under load.

Figure 1. An action travels through Table Storage, onto a queue, and only takes effect once its message is consumed. Every stage writes to the file share.

Placing an order writes it to the Orders table as Submitted and queues a message. Nothing else happens yet. Processing that message is what marks the order complete and takes the stock off the product, which in turn queues a stock movement on the inventory queue. A burst of Christmas orders therefore accumulates on a queue that is designed to absorb it, rather than contending for the same database rows, which is exactly the failure the brief describes.

Section 3

Queue design

QueueCarries
order-processing Orders waiting to be picked, packed and dispatched
inventory-management Catalogue and stock movements, including image uploads

Two queues rather than one, so that a backlog of catalogue edits cannot delay a customer's order. Each can also be given its own consumer, or scaled independently, without touching the other.

What a message carries

A queue message body is just a string. Each one therefore holds JSON with a readable description for the operator alongside the reference a consumer needs to act on it, so a single message serves both the monitoring screen and the processing code without a second lookup.

At-least-once delivery

Receiving a message does not remove it. Queue Storage hides it for a visibility timeout, and it is deleted only once the work has succeeded. A consumer that crashes part way through leaves the message to reappear and be retried, which is what makes the queue reliable rather than merely fast. The consequence is that a message can be delivered more than once, so the order handler checks whether an order is already complete before acting on it instead of assuming each message arrives exactly once.

Peek rather than receive for monitoring

The monitoring screen peeks at messages. Receiving them would start their visibility timeout and hide them from the code that is supposed to process them, so simply opening a dashboard would interfere with the workflow.

Section 4

Log files on Azure Files

Logs live on the application-logs file share rather than in a blob container. A share is a real SMB file system: it can be mounted as a drive on a server or a workstation and read with ordinary tools, which is what an operations team actually wants from a log. A blob would have to be downloaded first.

Appending, which Azure Files does not offer directly

Unlike an append blob, an Azure file has no append operation. Adding a line means reading the file's current length, growing the file by the size of the new bytes, and then writing those bytes into the range that growth created. That sequence is three calls and is not atomic, so writers are serialised within the application. Across several App Service instances the correct answer would be a lease on the file; on the single instance this runs on, serialising is enough and is documented as such rather than left implicit.

Logging never breaks the request

A failure writing to the share is reported to the platform log and swallowed, and the user's action is allowed to complete. A customer losing their order because the log file was momentarily busy would plainly be the worse outcome.

Section 5

Implementation

ComponentResponsibility
QueueStorageService Send, peek, dequeue, depth and clear over Azure.Storage.Queues.
FileShareService Append, write, list and read over Azure.Storage.Files.Shares.
ActivityRecorder Writes the queue message and the log line together.
OrdersController Places orders and produces order-processing messages.
QueuesController Monitors both queues and consumes messages off them.
LogsController Browses the share, reads log files and writes inventory reports.

Controllers never call the queue and the file services separately. They call IActivityRecorder, which pairs the two writes, so no caller can queue work and forget to log it. The queue write comes first and is allowed to fail loudly: work that never reached the queue must not be reported as queued.

Every client is a singleton. QueueClient and ShareClient are thread safe and pool their connections, so one instance for the lifetime of the application avoids the socket exhaustion that follows from constructing a client per request. All four storage services sit behind interfaces resolved through dependency injection, which is why this task was additive rather than a rewrite of the Task 1 application.

Section 8

Verification

The flow was exercised against the live storage account rather than assumed. Placing an order wrote the entity, raised the depth of order-processing and appended a log line. Processing that message marked the order complete, moved the stock for Aurora Wireless Headphones from 42 to 39, queued the resulting movement on inventory-management and logged both steps. Writing an inventory report produced a CSV in exports/. Each of those lines was then read back out of the share and rendered in the browser, which is what figure 5 shows.

The depth the site reports was checked against the storage account directly and matched: two messages on inventory-management and none on order-processing at the time of the check.
